domain: Storm God, Lord of the Heavens
meaning: Canaanite storm and fertility god; the title "Lord" (baʿlu) was also applied to local deities

phonemes.desc: Plain voiced bilabial [b] plus open [a]; the word means 'lord, owner, husband' across Semitic languages.
Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ] plus [a] and [l]. The pharyngeal is the signature consonant; we render it with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for registrability.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-ahl' — the middle consonant is a deep, throaty 'ʿ' (like Arabic ع), not a glottal stop or silent letter.

kin.label: Ugaritic
kin.form: 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (bʿl), 'lord'; as divine name often paired with Hadad/Haddu, the storm/thunder god

kin.label: Hebrew
kin.form: בַּעַל (Baʿal), 'lord, husband'; later a polemical name for Canaanite gods

kin.label: Akkadian
kin.form: Adad/Hadad (dIM), the storm god with whom Baꜥal was equated

pronunciation.note: Baꜥal is technically a title ('Lord') that became a name. The ideal form includes Semitic ʿayin, which is blocked at the DNS root; the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) is the registrable compromise. The name is Tier 1 because it preserves the ʿayin as a distinctive phoneme — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. In texts he is often 'Baꜥlu-Haddu' or simply the 'Rider on the Clouds.'

domains.title: Rider on the Clouds
domains.subtitle: Storm, Fertility, and Divine Kingship
domains.lead: Baꜥal is the storm made king. In a land where rain is life and drought is death, he is the deity who rides the clouds, shatters the sea-monster, and opens his palace windows so that the rains may fall. He is young, vigorous, and hungry for a throne — yet even his kingship depends on the older god Ēl. The Baꜥal Cycle is the great myth of his rise, death, and return.

cards.name: Storm and Thunder
cards.desc: His voice is thunder, his weapon lightning; he gathers clouds, wind, and rain around his chariot.

cards.name: Lord of Mount Zaphon
cards.desc: His cedar palace stands on the mountain of the north, the axis mundi from which he governs the cosmos.

cards.name: Fertility of Field and Flock
cards.desc: When he lives, bread, wine, and oil abound; when he descends to Mot, the land withers.

cards.name: Divine Warrior
cards.desc: He defeats Yamm, the primordial Sea, and shatters the seven-headed serpent Lotan.

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: His own victorious animal — he is acclaimed the 'bull' of the divine assembly — and the storm's fertile strength in one image

symbols.name: Lightning club
symbols.meaning: Yagrush and Ayamur, the twin maces Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs forged and named to shatter Yamm (KTU 1.2 iv)

symbols.name: Window
symbols.meaning: The palace window Baꜥal hesitated to cut; through it his thunder goes forth to the world (KTU 1.4 vii)

symbols.name: Cloud chariot
symbols.meaning: The storm cloud itself, his vehicle — 'Rider on the Clouds' (rkb ʿrpt) is his oldest epithet

mythology.lead: The Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6) is the central myth of Canaanite religion. It tells how Baꜥal wins kingship from the chaotic Sea, builds his palace, confronts Death, and returns to bring back the rains. The cycle is a seasonal drama of drought and renewal, but also a political statement about divine legitimacy.

myths.title: Against Prince Yamm
myths.text: Before Baꜥal could rule, the Sea had to be beaten. In the opening tablets of the cycle (KTU 1.1–1.2), Ēl grants kingship to Yamm, the deified ocean, whose emissaries stride into the divine assembly and demand that Baꜥal himself be delivered as a captive. Baꜥal longs to strike the envoys down, but Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs restrains him: to kill the messengers would break the protocol of the gods. Instead the craftsman forges two maces and names them Yagrush, 'Chaser', and Ayamur, 'Driver.' With them Baꜥal strikes Yamm in the skull and between the eyes; the Sea falls, 'scattered' across the floor of the assembly, and the gods at last seat Baꜥal at the feast he was denied (KTU 1.2 iv). The combat is the Levant's great chaoskampf: kingship is legitimate only once the primordial deep has been driven back beyond the harbor wall — a myth of order founded not on creation but on conquest of the waters.

myths.title: The Cedar House on Zaphon
myths.text: Victory leaves Baꜥal homeless: a king without a palace is a king without a throne. He sends ꜥAnat to plead before Ēl, but it is Asherah — the diplomatic wife of the old god — who finally secures the decree (KTU 1.4 iv–v). Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs raises a cedar palace on Mount Zaphon, the cosmic north mountain, and Baꜥal hosts the banquet of the gods. One decision troubles him: Kothar urges him to cut a window in the palace wall, and Baꜥal hesitates — the window will let his thunder out to the world, but it may also let something in. When at last he opens it, he cries aloud through it, and his voice rolls from the heavens to the deeps (KTU 1.4 vii). Read as theology in architecture, the palace myth says that divine rule needs a fixed cosmic center: the voice that brings rain must have a gate through which to go — and a house worth defending when Death comes calling.

myths.title: Death in the Mouth of Mot
myths.text: When the palace is finished, Death itself sends an invitation. Mōt — whose throat is a lion's and whose gullet is a whale's — demands that Baꜥal come down into the realm of dust and drought (KTU 1.5 i). Baꜥal obeys: he takes his clouds, winds, and rains with him, and the earth dries behind him. Ēl mourns on the ground, gashing himself with a stone knife; ꜥAnat searches the world for her brother, finds him dead, and buries him on Zaphon. Then she turns on Mot and takes him apart: 'with a sword she splits him, with a sieve she winnows him, with fire she burns him, with millstones she grinds him, in the field she scatters him' (KTU 1.6 ii 30–35). Baꜥal returns, and the rains return with him. The myth refuses to treat death as an ending: it is a season with a boundary, and grief armed becomes the force that pushes the boundary back.

myths.title: Protector of Ugarit
myths.text: Baꜥal was not only the hero of cosmic myth; the people of Ugarit prayed to him at their own walls. A ritual text from the royal archives (KTU 1.119), composed for a time of military danger, invokes Baꜥal to expel the besieger from 'your city Ugarit' and to drive the enemy from its gates. The storm god who had conquered the Sea was the natural patron of a maritime city: votive anchors and figurines from his temple at Ras Shamra show sailors entrusting themselves to the power that had once subdued Yamm. This is liturgy rather than narrative — the cycle's cosmic drama compressed into one urgent civic prayer — and it shows that for Ugarit the battle against chaos was never finished. It returned each season, each siege, and had to be won again by sacrifice and song. The temple and the city wall stood as two faces of one theology: order, once won, must be defended every day.

lore.syncretism: Baꜥal is inseparable from the older West Semitic storm god Hadad/Haddu; in texts and inscriptions the two names are often combined as Baꜥal-Haddu. In Mesopotamia he was equated with Adad (dIM), and in Egypt he influenced the Levantine storm god imported during the New Kingdom. The Greeks saw in him a Near Eastern Zeus, a sky-storm king, though they did not directly worship him. In the Hebrew Bible, Baꜥal became the archetype of apostasy, the 'false god' opposed by Elijah on Mount Carmel. Later Jewish and Christian tradition demonized the name, turning 'Baal' into a byword for idolatry and, in medieval occultism, for a class of demons.
lore.culturalLegacy: No Canaanite name was more reviled or more enduring than Baꜥal. The prophets of Israel spent generations attacking his cult, yet his imagery — the storm god who rides the clouds, defeats the sea, and sends rain — was quietly absorbed into the figure of Yahweh. In the New Testament, Beelzebub ('Lord of the Flies,' probably a distortion of Baꜥal-Zebul, 'Prince Baꜥal') becomes a name for Satan. In modern fantasy and occult literature, Baal persists as a demon-king. But beneath the polemic remains the old Levantine truth: a god of storm and fertility whose absence means drought and whose return means life.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Baꜥal is the god of the necessary storm. He does not create the world; he saves it from chaos, builds a house for his voice, and dies so that the cycle of rain may continue. His mythology is not about transcendence but about recurrence — the eternal return of the waters that make civilization possible.

In a warming world, Baꜥal's story takes on new weight. The storm is no longer merely symbolic; it is the weather that either nourishes or destroys. To remember Baꜥal is to remember that divine kingship, in the ancient imagination, was bound to the rains. The health of the cosmos and the legitimacy of the king rose and fell together. That is a theology we have not outgrown, however much we have renamed it.
lore.originalScriptNote: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (b-ʿ-l), literally 'lord.' The middle sign is ʿayin, a voiced pharyngeal fricative. Because Semitic ʿayin is blocked at the DNS root, PUNICODEX renders it with the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ / U+A724). In many contexts the name is an appellative rather than a personal name; at Ugarit the storm god is often called Baꜥlu-Haddu.

lore.archaeology: The Temple of Baal at Ugarit, excavated by Claude Schaeffer, yielded stelae, votive anchors, and the Baʿal Cycle tablets (KTU 1.1–1.6). The Karatepe bilingual pairs Baʿal with King Azatiwada in Phoenician and Luwian. At Palmyra the great Temple of Baal-Shamin dominated the city; at Carthage, Baʿal-Hammon received child sacrifice in the tophet sanctuary. Hazor, Megiddo, and Mount Carmel provide Levantine cultic contexts attacked by biblical polemic.
